title: Provisions for the road
hookLine: Rehras is said as work ends, like provisions for the night's journey

lines: A TIFFIN PACKED FOR THE NIGHT RUN.
cards: Late afternoon at a truck stop on the Grand Trunk Road. A driver is getting ready for the night run to Delhi. He fills a steel tiffin with rotis and dal, tops up a bottle of water, checks the tires, wipes the windshield.
Nobody would set out on a long dark road without packing first. The night is coming whether he's ready or not, so he gets ready. Sikhs have a prayer for exactly this moment of the day.

teach.h: REHRAS: SAID AS THE DAY'S WORK ENDS.
teach.b: The evening prayer is called Rehras. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, places it in the evening, after sunset. For many, that's when the day's work is done.

teach.h: RAH AND RAAS: THE ROAD AND ITS GOODS.
teach.b: The name is often explained from two old words: rah, the road or the way, and raas, the goods or capital a traveler carries. Provisions for the road.
Some teachers also hear in it a humble petition, the request of someone setting out.
Scholars discuss the exact roots, but the picture Sikhs give is clear: the day is a journey, night is the next stretch of it, and Rehras is what you pack. What's in the tiffin?

In the standard Rehat Maryada order, it begins with nine shabads from the opening pages of the Guru Granth Sahib. Five are grouped under the heading So Dar, the door, and four under So Purakh, that Being.

teach.h: SO DAR, SO PURAKH, CHAUPAI, ANAND.
teach.b: Then come the Benti Chaupai of Guru Gobind Singh, a short savaiya and a dohra, the six pauris of the Anand you've just learned, and two closing passages that end the Guru Granth Sahib itself, the Mundavani and a slok.
Some Sikh traditions recite a longer form, with more hymns added. Then, in many homes, Ardas. Over the next two weeks we'll unpack it, one piece a day.
For now, just notice the shape of the Sikh day. Morning prayers before the work starts. Rehras as the work ends.

how: Sikhs recite Rehras Sahib in the evening as the day's work ends, at home or in the gurdwara, often followed by Ardas; the Rehat Maryada lists its contents as nine shabads, the Benti Chaupai, a savaiya and dohra, six pauris of the Anand, the Mundavani and a slok.

o: the morning prayer said before work begins
a ritual meal eaten together at sunset
the evening prayer: provisions for the road

games.q: the evening prayer — tap the pairs.

s: Rehras is said first thing in the morning
the Rehat Maryada places it in the evening, after sunset.
the six pauris of the Anand are part of Rehras
the first five and the fortieth.
every Sikh tradition recites exactly the same length of Rehras
the Rehat Maryada gives a standard order; some traditions add more hymns.

games.q: you're a Sikh coming home as the workday ends. when does the Rehat Maryada place Rehras?
o: only on Sundays at the gurdwara.
games.why: Rehras is the evening prayer, said as work ends, like packing provisions for the night's stretch of the road.

practice: Imagine the end of your workday, the laptop closing, the apron coming off, the last email sent, and let your shoulders drop as if it's already happened.

Take a slow breath and ask what you need for the next stretch, the evening and the night: rest, patience, someone's voice. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, and let that be the first thing packed.
